passage: Kunal, why are you spitting out every seed like that? Ah, the tree-in-the-stomach story. Let me tell you something. When I was nine, in our school in Nashik, everybody in my class knew that if you swallowed a watermelon seed, a vine would grow out of your ears. Pushpa said it. Her sister said it. Even the watchman's daughter said it. I heard it so often it felt like knowing my own name. One summer I swallowed a seed by mistake and cried all evening, holding my ears. My father laughed and asked, "Bhavna, who told you?" I opened my mouth, and I couldn't answer. Everyone. Nobody. Now eat your watermelon, beta, seeds and all. I'm seventy-one, and look, no vines.

qa.q: What did Bhavna's class believe would happen if you swallowed a watermelon seed?
qa.a: A vine would grow out of your ears.

qa.q: Why did young Bhavna cry all evening after swallowing a seed by mistake?
qa.a: Bhavna truly believed the vine story, because hearing it so often had made it feel as certain as knowing one's own name.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Bhavna, and how could Kunal use it?
qa.a: When the father asked "who told you?" and Bhavna had no answer. Kunal could ask the same question about the seed story before believing it.

qa.q: How might Bhavna's father have seen the crying?
qa.a: He probably found it a little funny, knowing seeds don't grow vines, but his simple question helped Bhavna notice the story had no real source.

grounding: An elder recalls believing, at nine, a playground food story only because everyone kept repeating it.

passage: The power went out at school just as the rain started, and the van was late, so Kiran had to walk home. That meant passing the old peepal tree by the water tank. A lady in white sat there at dusk. Salma had said so, and Rafi, and the big boys in Class 7, and even the canteen uncle had laughed and said, "Don't stop there." Kiran had heard it maybe a hundred times. It felt as solid as the tank itself. Now Kiran stood at the corner, stomach tight. "Has anyone actually seen her?" Salma asked, sharing the umbrella. Kiran started to answer, then stopped. Nobody had. Everyone had only heard. They walked past together, fast, and saw only wet leaves and a stray dog.

qa.q: Who had told Kiran about the lady in white?
qa.a: Salma, Rafi, the big boys in Class 7, and even the canteen uncle.

qa.q: What does Kiran's tight stomach at the corner show?
qa.a: Kiran was truly scared 😰 because the story had been heard so many times that it felt as solid as the tank itself.

qa.q: Which question became the turning point, and how could Kiran use it again?
qa.a: Salma's "Has anyone actually seen her?" Kiran could ask it whenever a story feels true only because everyone keeps saying it.

qa.q: Why might Salma ask that question even though Salma had helped spread the story?
qa.a: Standing near the real tree in the rain, Salma may have begun to doubt it, and asking aloud helped both friends feel brave enough to walk past.

grounding: A child walking home in rain and a power cut fears a ghost story heard so often it feels true, until a friend asks who has actually seen it.

passage: "If you eat enough carrots, you can see in the dark," Saurabh announced at the colony park. "Everyone knows." He had heard it from Anu on the swings, from two boys in his school van, and from a cousin at a wedding. It had come round so many times that it sat in his head next to "seven days in a week". Chetan, who was eleven, frowned. "Who told you first?" "Everyone." "Which book?" Saurabh opened his mouth and shut it again. That evening he ate four carrots, switched off his room light and stood very still. He could not see his cupboard. Then he sat on the bed, thinking about all the voices that had said it, and how none of them had ever tried.

qa.q: How many carrots did Saurabh eat that evening?
qa.a: Four carrots.

qa.q: What was Saurabh thinking about as he sat on the bed?
qa.a: All the voices that had repeated the carrot claim and how none of them had tried it, so he was beginning to doubt a "fact" that had felt certain 🤔

qa.q: What turning point led Saurabh to test the carrot fact?
qa.a: Chetan asking "Who told you first?" and "Which book?" Saurabh could not name a source, which pushed him to try it himself.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Saurabh's announcement at the park?
qa.a: Chetan seems doubtful and wants to know where the idea came from, rather than believing it just because Saurabh says everyone knows.

grounding: A boy believes a food "fact" because he has heard it from many people, until he is asked for its source and tests it.

passage:
"Bhupen Bhaiya, don't swallow it!"
"Swallow what?"
"The gum! It stays in your stomach for seven years."
Bhupen kept chewing. "Says who?"
"Everyone! Rukhsana, Mehul, both the twins, the van uncle. I've heard it like fifty times."
"Fifty times. And has anyone seen a seven-year-old piece of gum?"
Sabina frowned. "No, but everyone knows it."
"Everyone knows it, or everyone says it?"
"Same thing."
"Is it?"
Ammi called from the kitchen, "What's my girl shouting about?"
"Gum, Ammi! Seven years! It's true, na?"
"I've heard that too," Ammi said. "Never checked."
Sabina looked from one to the other. "But it feels so true."
"That's the funny part," Bhupen said, and dropped the gum into a wrapper. "Let's ask your science teacher on Monday."

qa.q: How many times did Sabina say she had heard the gum fact?
qa.a: She said she had heard it "like fifty times."

qa.q: Why does the gum fact feel so true to Sabina?
qa.a: She has heard it from so many people so often that it feels familiar, and familiar feels like true, even though no one has seen it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation, and what could Sabina do with it?
qa.a: Bhupen's question "Everyone knows it, or everyone says it?" made her pause; she could now check it with her science teacher on Monday.

qa.q: How might Ammi's answer affect Sabina?
qa.a: Hearing even Ammi say "Never checked" might surprise Sabina and show her that grown-ups repeat things without checking too.

grounding: A child believes a food 'fact' because everyone repeats it; familiarity makes it feel true.

passage: I'm Naveen, and until last year I believed that eating bread crusts gives you curly hair. Everyone in my class said it. Suraj said it, the twins said it, my cousin in Pune said it on the phone. I heard it so often it stopped feeling like a story and started feeling like a fact, like the sky being blue. So I ate every crust and checked the mirror. My hair stayed straight as sticks. Then one day in the library Suraj asked, "Who actually got curly hair from crusts?" We went round the class in our heads. Nobody. And Suraj's own hair is curly, and he hates crusts. We laughed until the librarian shushed us.

qa.q: What did Naveen believe about eating bread crusts?
qa.a: That eating bread crusts gives you curly hair.

qa.q: Why did the crust fact feel true to Naveen?
qa.a: Naveen felt certain and comfortable with it, because hearing it from so many people so often made it as familiar as the sky being blue.

qa.q: What question helped Naveen see through the fact, and when could it help again?
qa.a: Suraj's "Who actually got curly hair from crusts?" is worth asking whenever something is repeated a lot but no one has seen it happen.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt hearing the crust fact all those years with his curly hair?
qa.a: Suraj may have found it quietly funny, since he hated crusts and still had curly hair, which was proof against it all along.

grounding: A child believes a food 'fact' because everyone repeats it, until a friend asks who has actually seen it.

passage:
"Don't go near the old tank room," Imran said, stopping at the corner of the school building.
Harsha laughed. "Why?"
"There's a ghost. A boy who drowned in the tank. Everyone knows."
"Who told you?"
"Everyone! Sameer told me. And the Class 6 kids. And the auto uncle said it too. I've heard it like a hundred times."
"But did anyone see it?"
Imran hesitated. "No... but it's true. You can feel it."
"How can a thing be true just because everyone says it?"
"Because..." Imran kicked a stone. "Because it just sounds true. I've heard it so much."
Harsha walked right up to the door and knocked. Nothing. Imran didn't move from the corner.

qa.q: Who did Imran say had told him about the ghost?
qa.a: Sameer, the Class 6 kids and the auto uncle.

qa.q: Why did Imran stay at the corner when Harsha knocked?
qa.a: He felt scared and uneasy, because the ghost story felt true to him after hearing it so many times.

qa.q: What question could help Imran think about the ghost story?
qa.a: Asking "Has anyone actually seen it, or have they only heard it?" could help him notice that hearing a thing often is not the same as proof.

qa.q: How does Harsha see the ghost story?
qa.a: Harsha seems curious and unafraid, treating it as something to test rather than believe because it is repeated.

grounding: It shows a child believing a ghost story because it has been repeated so often that it feels familiar and true.

passage:
I'm Tanuja, and in Class 3 I believed that if you swallowed a watermelon seed, a watermelon would grow in your stomach.
Gautam said it first, at lunch. Then my cousin said it. Then the girls at the bus stop. By summer I had heard it so many times that it felt like a thing everyone just knew, like the sky being blue.
So I ate watermelon very carefully, picking out every seed with my fingers. Once I swallowed one by mistake and cried in the bathroom. I didn't tell anyone.
Later our science teacher explained how seeds need soil and sunlight to grow. I felt silly, and also a bit cheated.
It's funny. I never checked. It just sounded right because I'd heard it everywhere.

qa.q: Who said the watermelon seed fact first?
qa.a: Gautam said it first, at lunch.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling after swallowing a seed by mistake?
qa.a: Tanuja felt frightened and alone, crying in the bathroom without telling anyone.

qa.q: What could Tanuja have done when the worry started?
qa.a: Tanuja could have asked a trusted adult or the science teacher whether it was true, instead of carrying the fear alone.

qa.q: What would change if Tanuja had heard the seed fact only once?
qa.a: It would probably have felt less familiar and less true, so Tanuja might have doubted it or asked about it sooner.

grounding: It shows a child believing a food "fact" because friends repeated it so often that it felt true.

passage:
Class 5B, observation note, Tuesday.
Santosh would not use the second-floor washroom today. He ran to the ground floor at break and was late back. When I asked, he said quietly that a woman in white appears in the mirror if you go alone.
I asked where he heard it. "Everyone says it, ma'am. Sabina's brother saw it." Sabina, sitting nearby, said her brother hadn't seen it, he had heard it from someone in Class 8.
Santosh looked confused. "But everybody knows it," he said, as though that settled it.
What I did next: I walked with Santosh and Sabina to the washroom, we switched on the light and looked at the mirror together. Tomorrow I'll talk with the class about how things feel true when we hear them many times.

qa.q: Which washroom would Santosh not use?
qa.a: He would not use the second-floor washroom.

qa.q: What does Santosh's reply "But everybody knows it" suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt frightened and sure, because hearing the story over and over made it feel like a known fact.

qa.q: How does the note-writer's plan for tomorrow help?
qa.a: Talking with the class about how repeated stories feel true can help children question "facts" they only heard, instead of just fearing them.

qa.q: How does Sabina seem to see the story once she hears her brother's name?
qa.a: She seems to want to set it straight, pointing out that her brother only heard it from someone else and never saw it.

grounding: It shows a child believing a ghost "fact" because everyone repeats it, as noted by an adult who watched.

passage:
Dear diary,
Disaster. I swallowed my gum in PT. Dilnaz screamed, "Now it'll stay in your stomach for SEVEN YEARS!" Everyone knows that. My cousin says it, the bus boys say it, even Dilnaz's big sister. I've heard it about a hundred times, so it must be true.
I kept touching my tummy all through maths.
At home I told Mummy, almost crying. She laughed a little, then hugged me and said it just passes through like food, and if my tummy ever hurts I should tell her. She said lots of things people repeat aren't true; they only sound true because we've heard them so often.
I still feel weird. But Mummy doesn't lie.
Preeti

qa.q: Where did Preeti swallow the gum?
qa.a: In PT.

qa.q: Why was Preeti so sure the gum would stay for seven years?
qa.a: Preeti felt scared and certain, because hearing it so many times made it feel true.

qa.q: What could Preeti ask the next time a playground fact is scary?
qa.a: Where it comes from, and whether someone who really knows, like Mummy or a teacher, agrees.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel if she learned the fact was wrong?
qa.a: Dilnaz might feel surprised and a bit sheepish, having shouted it so confidently.

grounding: A child's diary shows believing a food 'fact' because everyone repeats it, as familiarity makes it feel true.

passage:
In Harsha's village, every child knew that if you swallowed a watermelon seed, a plant would grow in your stomach. The older boys said it at the pond, the girls said it at the handpump, and even the bangle-seller joked about it at the fair.
So when Harsha swallowed a seed at his cousin Payal's house in the summer holidays, he went pale. "It'll grow out of my mouth," he whispered.
Payal, who was in Class 8 and read everything, laughed. "It doesn't work like that. Seeds need soil and light."
Harsha didn't believe her. Everybody had said it, so many times. For three days he checked his tongue in the mirror every morning.

qa.q: Where did Harsha swallow the seed?
qa.a: At his cousin Payal's house in the summer holidays.

qa.q: Why didn't Harsha believe Payal?
qa.a: He felt frightened, and the 'fact' felt truer because he had heard it from everyone so many times.

qa.q: What could help Harsha trust the real explanation?
qa.a: Checking with a teacher or a book, and noticing that hearing something often doesn't make it true.

qa.q: How might Payal feel watching Harsha check his tongue?
qa.a: Payal might feel amused but also a little sorry for how scared he is.

grounding: Shows a village child believing a food 'fact' because everyone repeats it, so it feels truer than a correct explanation.

passage:
At her school in Madrid, Yuki heard it in her first week: the last toilet on the second floor was haunted, and if you knocked three times, a cold hand touched your shoulder. Pablo said it. Then Lucia. Then the twins. By the end of the month Yuki had heard it maybe twenty times, and it felt as true as her own address. She walked all the way down to the ground-floor toilet, even in the rain.
When the teacher asked the class who had actually felt the hand, nobody raised theirs. "But everyone says it," Yuki said. Pablo shrugged. "My brother told me."
Yuki still took the stairs down. Knowing nobody had felt it didn't stop it feeling true.

qa.q: Which toilet was said to be haunted?
qa.a: The last toilet on the second floor.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when she still took the stairs down?
qa.a: She still felt uneasy and scared, because the story felt familiar and so felt true.

qa.q: What could the teacher do next to help the class?
qa.a: Talk about how hearing something often makes it feel true, and perhaps visit the toilet together to show it's ordinary.

qa.q: How does Pablo seem to feel about the story now?
qa.a: Pablo seems unbothered, shrugging and passing it off on his brother.

grounding: Shows a child believing a ghost story because classmates repeat it so often that its familiarity makes it feel true.

passage: On the first hot day of summer term at the Bhopal school, the canteen line buzzed with the same news: if you swallow a watermelon seed, a watermelon grows inside you. Lalit heard it from Binita in the morning. At recess three more children said it. By lunch, a boy in 6C swore his cousin had needed an operation. Lalit had laughed at breakfast. By the last bell, he was carefully spitting every seed out of his watermelon slice onto a napkin, and he felt a small wobble in his tummy whenever he thought about the one he'd swallowed last week. When the science teacher heard, she smiled and said, 'Seeds don't grow in stomachs.' Lalit nodded, but he still spat out the seeds.

qa.q: What did the children say happens if you swallow a watermelon seed?
qa.a: A watermelon grows inside you.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel thinking about the seed he swallowed last week?
qa.a: Lalit felt worried, with a small wobble in his tummy, because the story had started to feel true after hearing it so often.

qa.q: What could Lalit ask himself the next time a 'fact' spreads?
qa.a: Where it came from and who actually knows, instead of believing it because many people repeat it.

qa.q: How might the science teacher see the children's worry?
qa.a: The teacher finds it amusing but also sees how quickly a repeated story can feel true to children.

grounding: A child believes a 'fact' because everyone repeats it; hearing it often makes it feel familiar and true.

passage:
Monday, the first day of the Christmas holidays. At the colony gate, Zubin told Hansa, 'If you whistle at night, ghosts come.' Hansa laughed. 'That's silly.'

Wednesday. Hansa heard it again from the twins upstairs and from the vegetable seller's son. Everyone said it the same way. She didn't laugh this time.

Friday night. Walking back from the carol singing, Hansa's little brother started whistling. Hansa grabbed his arm. 'Stop! Ghosts!' He stared at her. 'Who said?' She opened her mouth. 'Everyone.' 'But who saw a ghost?' Hansa couldn't answer. She still made him stop whistling.

qa.q: What did Zubin say happens if you whistle at night?
qa.a: Ghosts come.

qa.q: Why did Hansa grab her brother's arm on Friday night?
qa.a: Hansa felt scared, because hearing the saying from so many people had made it feel true.

qa.q: What question could help Hansa think it through?
qa.a: Her brother's question, 'But who saw a ghost?', helps her notice that repetition is not the same as proof.

qa.q: How might Hansa's brother see her sudden fear?
qa.a: Her brother is puzzled, since he has not heard the saying so often and just wants to know who saw a ghost.

grounding: Over a week, a child comes to believe a ghost 'fact' because everyone repeats it, so it feels familiar and true.

passage: Gurleen beti, you won't sit under the tamarind tree because 'everyone says' a ghost lives there? Let me, your Zeenat Nani, tell you a story. The Eid I was nine, in Lucknow, all my cousins said that if you ate a sweet before namaz, you'd get worms. My older cousin said it. The girls next door said it. Even the halwai's son said it. I didn't believe it at first. By the third time I heard it, I was sure. That whole Eid morning I didn't touch a single sevaiyan until after namaz, and I was so hungry I cried. My Abbu laughed and asked who had got worms from sevaiyan. I couldn't name one person. Only that everyone said so. That's when I learned, beti: hearing something many times makes it feel true, but it doesn't make it true.

qa.q: What did Zeenat's cousins say would happen if you ate a sweet before namaz?
qa.a: You'd get worms.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel that Eid morning?
qa.a: Zeenat felt so hungry and worried that she cried, because the repeated claim had come to feel true.

qa.q: What question inside the story changed Zeenat's mind?
qa.a: Abbu asking who had actually got worms from sevaiyan, which showed nobody could name a single case.

qa.q: How might Abbu have seen young Zeenat's refusal?
qa.a: Abbu found it funny and a little sweet, and used a gentle question to help her think.

grounding: An elder recalls believing a food 'fact' because everyone repeated it, until asked for a single real example.

passage:
The power went out on Christmas Eve just as the carol group reached the end of the lane, and someone had to fetch candles from Francis's house, past the old well.
"Not me," Francis said, gripping the gate. "The white lady sits on that well after dark. Everybody knows."
Vandana, holding the matchbox, asked, "Who actually saw her?"
Francis opened his mouth. Vandana herself had told him in Class 2. The big boys said it every monsoon. Even the bakery aunty joked about it. He had heard it a hundred times, so it felt as solid as the well itself.
But nobody, he realised, had ever said, "I saw her."
Still, his feet did not move. The carols waited in the dark.

qa.q: Where did someone have to go to fetch candles?
qa.a: To Francis's house, past the old well.

qa.q: Why does the story about the white lady feel true to Francis?
qa.a: He has heard it so many times, from Vandana, the big boys and the bakery aunty, that it feels familiar and solid, so he stays scared even though nobody ever saw her.

qa.q: What small step could help Francis test the story?
qa.a: He could ask each person where they heard it, notice that no one says "I saw her", and then walk to the well with Vandana and a torch.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel when Francis repeats a story she once told him?
qa.a: She may feel a bit guilty or amused, realising her Class 2 tale has become something Francis now treats as fact.

grounding: Shows a child believing a ghost story because it has been repeated so often that it feels familiar and therefore true.
